core.h: Other factors affecting rate of cooling
core.p: Thickness and thermal conductivity are the two factors the spec names, but a full answer recognises that other factors matter too. Use these only to support your explanation, not to replace the named factors.
bullets: **Temperature difference**: the bigger the difference between inside and outside, the faster the building cools
**Surface area**: a larger area of wall, roof or window lets more energy escape per second
**Draughts**: gaps let warm air escape by convection
Windows usually lose energy faster than walls because glass is thin and has a higher thermal conductivity than an insulated wall

core.p: The same ideas apply to many everyday objects designed to keep things hot or cold.
bullets: **Vacuum flask**: a vacuum between double walls stops conduction and convection; silvered surfaces reduce radiation; a stopper reduces convection and evaporation
**Kettle**: a plastic or insulated body reduces energy transfer to the kitchen, so more energy heats the water
**Hot water tank jacket**: thick insulating layer keeps stored water hot
**Clothing**: layers trap air, reducing energy transfer from the body
**Cool box**: insulation slows energy transfer from the warm surroundings into the food

core.p: A common class investigation compares insulating materials. Beakers of hot water are wrapped in different materials (or different thicknesses of the same material) and their temperatures are recorded over time. The slower the temperature falls, the better the insulation.
bullets: Independent variable: type of insulating material or number of layers (thickness)
Dependent variable: temperature drop in a fixed time (or rate of cooling)
Control variables: starting temperature, volume of water, size of beaker, room temperature, time, use of a lid
Use a thermometer or temperature probe and a stopwatch; read at regular intervals
Plot temperature against time; the shallower curve shows the better insulator
Safety: take care handling hot water to avoid scalds

callouts.p: If a question asks how to make the investigation fair, give specific control variables such as 'same starting temperature' and 'same volume of water', not just 'keep everything the same'.

analogy.p: Think of energy trying to get out of a warm house as people leaving a packed stadium. Thermal conductivity is like how easy each exit corridor is to walk through: a wide, clear corridor (high conductivity) lets people out quickly, a cluttered one (low conductivity) slows them. Wall thickness is the length of the corridor: a longer corridor takes longer to get through, so fewer people leave each minute. Lubrication is like oiling the turnstiles so they turn without grinding. Where it breaks down: energy is not a crowd of objects travelling through the wall; in conduction it is passed from particle to particle by vibrations, and insulation only slows the rate rather than locking any energy inside.

terms.d: An energy transfer to a store that is not useful, such as heating the surroundings.
A force that opposes motion between surfaces; work done against it transfers energy to thermal stores.
A substance such as oil or grease placed between moving surfaces to reduce friction.
Using a lubricant to reduce friction so that less energy is dissipated by heating.
A material with low thermal conductivity that reduces the rate of energy transfer by heating.
Material or design used to reduce the rate of unwanted energy transfer by heating.
A measure of how quickly a material transfers energy through it by conduction.
Energy transfer through a material by vibrating particles passing energy to neighbouring particles.
Energy transfer in a fluid (liquid or gas) when warmer, less dense fluid rises and cooler fluid sinks.
Electromagnetic radiation emitted by all objects; hotter objects emit more per second.
How quickly the temperature of an object falls, linked to the rate of energy transfer from it.
The amount of energy transferred per second.
Insulating foam injected into the gap between the two layers of a brick wall, trapping air and reducing energy transfer.
Windows with two panes of glass separated by a layer of air or gas, reducing energy transfer by conduction.
Shaping an object so that it has less air resistance, reducing energy wasted when it moves.
The difference in temperature between two places; a larger difference gives a faster rate of energy transfer.

mistakes.w: Insulation stops heat escaping.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces the rate of energy transfer; it cannot stop it completely.

mistakes.w: Insulation keeps the cold out.
mistakes.r: Insulation reduces energy transfer from the warm inside to the cooler outside.

mistakes.w: Lubrication removes friction.
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the surfaces.

mistakes.w: Thicker walls have higher thermal conductivity so they keep the house warm.
mistakes.r: Thermal conductivity is a property of the material, not the thickness; thicker walls give a lower rate of energy transfer.

mistakes.w: Materials with high thermal conductivity are good insulators.
mistakes.r: Good insulators have low thermal conductivity.

mistakes.w: Air is a good insulator, so a large open gap in a wall is best.
mistakes.r: Air must be trapped in small pockets; in a large gap convection currents can transfer energy.

mistakes.w: Oil makes the machine use less energy because the energy is saved in the oil.
mistakes.r: Oil reduces friction so less energy is wasted by heating; more of the input is transferred usefully.

mistakes.w: Double glazing works because glass is an insulator.
mistakes.r: The sealed layer of air or gas between the panes has a low thermal conductivity, reducing conduction.

exam.q: State one way of reducing unwanted energy transfer in a machine with moving parts.
model: Lubricate the moving parts (with oil or grease).
exam.tip: Lubrication is the spec answer; streamlining is acceptable for air resistance.

exam.q: Explain how oiling a bicycle chain reduces the energy wasted.
model: Oil reduces friction between the chain and the gears.
So less energy is transferred to the thermal store of the chain / dissipated to the surroundings.
exam.tip: Two linked ideas: friction down, heating down.

exam.q: Which material, copper or polystyrene, has the lower thermal conductivity?
model: Polystyrene.
exam.tip: Insulators have low thermal conductivity.

exam.q: Describe the effect of increasing the thickness of a building's walls on its rate of cooling.
model: The rate of energy transfer through the walls decreases.
So the building cools more slowly / the rate of cooling decreases.
exam.tip: Describe qualitatively: use 'decreases' or 'more slowly'.

exam.q: Describe the effect of building walls from a material with a higher thermal conductivity.
model: Energy is transferred through the walls faster / higher rate of energy transfer.
So the building cools faster.
exam.tip: Higher conductivity means faster cooling.

exam.q: Explain how cavity wall insulation reduces energy transfer from a house.
model: Foam traps air in small pockets.
Air is a poor conductor / foam has low thermal conductivity, reducing conduction.
Air cannot move, so convection currents in the cavity are prevented.
exam.tip: Mention both conduction and convection for full marks.

exam.q: Explain why double glazing reduces energy transfer through a window.
model: The gap between the panes contains air or gas, which has a low thermal conductivity.
This reduces the rate of energy transfer by conduction.
exam.tip: It is the trapped gas, not the extra glass, that matters.

exam.q: A student wants to compare how well two insulating materials work. Describe a method she could use.
model: Wrap identical beakers of hot water in each material.
Use the same volume of water and the same starting temperature.
Measure the temperature with a thermometer at regular intervals / after a fixed time.
The material giving the smaller temperature drop is the better insulator.
exam.tip: Include control variables and how to judge the result.

exam.q: Explain why a lubricated machine is more efficient than an unlubricated one.
model: Lubricant reduces friction between moving parts.
Less work is done against friction, so less energy is dissipated by heating.
So a greater proportion of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.
exam.tip: Link to 'proportion of input energy' for efficiency.

exam.q: A family wants to reduce their heating bills. Explain how the design of the walls and other features of the house could reduce the rate of energy transfer from the house.
model: Thicker walls reduce the rate of energy transfer, so the house cools more slowly.
Walls made from materials with lower thermal conductivity reduce the rate of energy transfer by conduction.
Cavity wall insulation traps air in foam, reducing conduction and preventing convection in the cavity.
Loft insulation traps air, reducing energy transfer through the roof.
Double glazing has a gas layer of low thermal conductivity between panes; draught excluders stop warm air escaping by convection.
Less energy needs to be supplied by the heating to keep the house warm, so bills are lower.
exam.tip: Cover both named wall factors first, then other methods, then link to lower bills.

worked.q: Two identical houses are heated to 20 °C and the heating is switched off. House A has thin walls made of brick. House B has thick walls with a layer of foam inside. Compare how the houses cool.
steps: Both houses transfer energy to the colder surroundings.
House B has thicker walls, so energy must be conducted further through them, giving a lower rate of energy transfer.
Foam has a lower thermal conductivity than brick, which further reduces the rate.
So House B has a lower rate of cooling and its temperature falls more slowly than House A.
worked.ans: House B cools more slowly because its walls are thicker and contain a low thermal conductivity material.

worked.q: In a class experiment, beaker X (no insulation) falls from 80 °C to 56 °C in 10 minutes; beaker Y (wrapped in wool) falls from 80 °C to 68 °C in the same time. Compare the average rates of cooling.
steps: Temperature drop of X = 80 - 56 = 24 °C.
Average rate for X = 24 °C / 10 min = 2.4 °C per minute.
Temperature drop of Y = 80 - 68 = 12 °C.
Average rate for Y = 12 °C / 10 min = 1.2 °C per minute.
Y cools at half the rate of X because the wool traps air, which has a low thermal conductivity.
worked.ans: X: 2.4 °C/min, Y: 1.2 °C/min, so the wool halves the rate of cooling.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a car engine needs oil.
steps: Inside the engine, metal parts such as pistons slide against each other.
Friction between them would transfer a lot of energy to their thermal store, causing them to heat up and wear.
Oil forms a thin layer that separates the surfaces and reduces friction.
Less energy is dissipated by heating, so more of the energy from the fuel is transferred to the kinetic store of the car.
worked.ans: Oil reduces friction between moving parts, so less energy is wasted by heating and the engine is more efficient.

phy_edx.2.4.summary: **Efficiency** tells you what fraction of the energy supplied to a device is transferred usefully. Edexcel requires you to recall and use **efficiency = useful energy transferred by the device / total energy supplied to the device**, giving answers as a decimal or a percentage, and to explain how efficiency can be increased. Because some energy is always dissipated to the surroundings, no real device is 100% efficient, but reducing friction, insulating and redesigning devices can make far more of the input useful.

core.p: Every device takes in energy and transfers some of it to a useful store and the rest to wasted stores, usually the thermal store of the surroundings. **Efficiency** compares the useful output with the total input. A device with a high efficiency transfers a large proportion of its input usefully and wastes only a little.
bullets: Efficiency is a **ratio**: useful output compared with total input
An efficiency of 0.8 (80%) means 80% of the input is transferred usefully and 20% is wasted
Higher efficiency = less energy wasted for the same useful job
Efficiency depends on what counts as useful: a heater that warms a room is very efficient because the heating is the useful output

core.p: You must **recall** this equation; it is not given on the Edexcel equation sheet. Both energies must be in the **same unit** (usually joules, J), so the units cancel.
bullets: efficiency = useful energy transferred by the device / total energy supplied to the device
Useful energy and total energy are both measured in joules (J)
The total energy supplied is the input energy, which always equals useful energy + wasted energy
Always write the equation, substitute, then calculate: each stage can earn a mark

callouts.p: efficiency = (useful energy transferred by the device) / (total energy supplied to the device)
This equation is one you must remember. Write it out in full at the start of every efficiency calculation.

core.p: The equation gives a decimal between 0 and 1. To turn it into a percentage, multiply by 100. Efficiency has **no units**, because it is joules divided by joules.
bullets: Decimal form: 0.65
Percentage form: 0.65 x 100 = 65%
Never write 'J' after an efficiency
Give the form the question asks for; if it does not say, either is fine but do not mix them up (0.65% is wrong)
Efficiency can never be greater than 1 (100%): that would mean creating energy, which breaks conservation of energy
If your answer is greater than 1, you have put the numbers the wrong way up

callouts.p: Useful goes on TOP. If you get 1.25 or 125%, swap the numbers.

fig.cap: Efficiency always lies between 0 and 1 (0% and 100%) and has no units. A kettle with efficiency 0.9 transfers 90% of its input usefully. An answer above 1 is impossible.

core.p: Questions often give you the efficiency and ask for the useful energy or the total energy supplied. Rearrange before substituting. If the efficiency is given as a percentage, convert it to a decimal first by dividing by 100.
bullets: useful energy = efficiency x total energy supplied
total energy supplied = useful energy / efficiency
Convert 40% to 0.40 before using it
Check: the useful energy must always be smaller than the total supplied

callouts.p: Dividing by an efficiency (less than 1) makes the number bigger, which is right for total input. Multiplying by an efficiency makes the number smaller, which is right for useful output.

fig.cap: Equation triangle for efficiency. Cover the quantity you want: useful = efficiency x total; efficiency = useful / total; total = useful / efficiency.

core.h: Finding useful energy from wasted energy
core.p: Some questions give the total energy and the wasted energy instead of the useful energy. Use conservation of energy first, then the efficiency equation.
bullets: Step 1: useful energy = total energy supplied - wasted energy
Step 2: efficiency = useful / total
Alternatively: efficiency = 1 - (wasted / total)
Watch the units: convert kJ to J (x 1000) or make sure both are in kJ

callouts.p: A common error is wasted / total. That gives the fraction wasted, not the efficiency.

core.p: Power is the energy transferred per second, so you can also calculate efficiency using power values, as long as both are measured over the same time. This is useful when a question gives the input and output in watts.
bullets: efficiency = useful power output / total power input
Both powers in watts (W) or both in kilowatts (kW)
Example: a motor with 400 W input and 300 W useful output has efficiency 300 / 400 = 0.75
The same rules apply: no units, never above 1

core.p: In every real energy transfer, some energy is **dissipated** to the surroundings. Moving parts experience friction and air resistance, currents heat wires, and hot objects transfer energy to cooler surroundings. So the useful energy is always less than the total energy supplied and the efficiency is always less than 1.
bullets: Friction between moving parts heats them
Electrical resistance heats wires and components
Sound is produced by vibrating parts
Hot parts transfer energy to the surroundings by conduction, convection and radiation
Energy is conserved: total input = useful output + wasted output

callouts.p: Efficiency below 100% does not mean energy is destroyed. The 'missing' energy is in the thermal store of the surroundings.

core.p: In a Sankey diagram the width of each arrow is proportional to the energy. Read off the input and the useful output (count squares if a grid is drawn), then use the efficiency equation.
bullets: Input = width of the arrow coming in
Useful = width of the arrow going straight on
Efficiency = useful width / input width
Check that useful + wasted = input

fig.cap: Sankey diagram for an electric kettle. 2000 J is supplied, 1800 J goes to the thermal store of the water and 200 J is dissipated to the surroundings. Efficiency = 1800 / 2000 = 0.9 (90%).

core.h: How to increase efficiency: the principle
core.p: To increase efficiency you must **reduce the wasted energy**, so that a greater proportion of the energy supplied is transferred to the useful store. You do this by identifying where energy is being dissipated and then reducing that unwanted transfer.
bullets: Identify the wasted pathway: friction, air resistance, electrical heating, sound, heating of surroundings
Reduce that pathway with lubrication, streamlining, insulation or better design
For the same input, more useful output; or for the same useful output, less input needed
State the result in terms of the equation: useful energy is a larger fraction of total energy supplied

callouts.p: For each method, say what it reduces and why that raises efficiency, for example 'lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated by heating, so more of the input is transferred usefully'.

fig.cap: The same 100 J is supplied to a machine before and after its moving parts are lubricated. Lubrication reduces the wasted energy from 40 J to 25 J, so the useful energy rises from 60 J to 75 J and the efficiency rises from 60% to 75%.

core.p: Match each method to the wasted energy it reduces. These are the examples most often rewarded in mark schemes.
bullets: Methods that reduce friction or air resistance help mechanical devices
Methods that reduce heating losses help thermal devices and buildings
Better components (such as LEDs) help electrical devices

head: Method
What it reduces
Example
rows: Friction between moving parts, so less heating
Energy transfer by heating to the surroundings
Kettle body, hot water tank jacket, loft insulation
Using LEDs instead of filament lamps
Heating of the lamp; more input transferred as light

core.p: Choosing efficient devices has real consequences. Exam questions may ask you to compare two devices or justify a choice.
bullets: Less energy needs to be supplied for the same useful output, so running costs are lower
Less fuel is burned in power stations, so fewer fossil fuels are used up
Less carbon dioxide is released, reducing contribution to climate change
When comparing devices, also consider purchase cost, lifetime and payback time, not just efficiency
A more efficient device can cost more to buy but save money over its lifetime

core.p: Efficiency questions are usually 2 or 3 marks. Follow the same routine every time and you will pick up method marks even if you slip on the arithmetic.
bullets: Write the equation in words or symbols
Convert units so useful and total are the same (J and J, or kJ and kJ)
Convert percentages to decimals before rearranging
Substitute the numbers
Give the answer as a decimal or percentage, as asked, with no units
Check the answer is between 0 and 1 (0% and 100%)

callouts.p: Mark schemes award a mark for correct substitution, so write 'efficiency = 300 / 400' before the answer.

analogy.p: Imagine you are given 10 pounds (total energy supplied) to buy a book (the useful job). On the way, some coins fall through a hole in your pocket (wasted energy). If you arrive with 8 pounds to spend, your 'efficiency' is 8 / 10 = 0.8. Sewing up the hole (lubrication, insulation) means more of the money reaches the shop, so efficiency goes up. You can never arrive with more than you started with, just as efficiency can never exceed 1. Where it breaks down: the lost coins are gone from you but still exist somewhere, just as wasted energy still exists in the surroundings; however, unlike coins, dissipated energy is spread so thinly that it can never practically be picked up again.

terms.d: The proportion of the total energy supplied to a device that is transferred usefully: useful energy / total energy supplied.
Energy transferred to the store the device is designed to fill.
All the energy put into the device (the input energy).
Energy transferred to stores that are not useful, usually the thermal store of the surroundings.
Spreading out of energy into the surroundings so it is stored in less useful ways.
The rate of energy transfer, measured in watts (W); 1 W = 1 J/s.
The unit of energy.
Efficiency multiplied by 100 to give a value between 0% and 100%.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so total input = useful output + wasted output.
Using oil or grease to reduce friction between moving parts, reducing wasted energy.
A material with low thermal conductivity that reduces unwanted energy transfer by heating.
Shaping an object to reduce air resistance.
An energy transfer diagram with arrow widths proportional to the amount of energy.
A force opposing motion between surfaces; work done against it heats the surfaces.
The time taken for the money saved by an efficiency improvement to equal its cost.

mistakes.w: efficiency = total / useful
mistakes.r: efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy supplied; useful goes on top.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = 0.75 J
mistakes.r: Efficiency has no units: 0.75 or 75%.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = 120%
mistakes.r: Efficiency can never be more than 100%; check the fraction is not upside down.

mistakes.w: Using 40 instead of 0.40 for a 40% efficiency when rearranging.
mistakes.r: Convert the percentage to a decimal (divide by 100) before using it.

mistakes.w: Efficiency = wasted / total
mistakes.r: That is the fraction wasted; efficiency uses useful energy on the top.

mistakes.w: Mixing kJ and J in the same fraction.
mistakes.r: Convert so useful and total energy are in the same unit.

mistakes.w: Making a device more efficient creates more energy.
mistakes.r: It reduces wasted energy, so a greater proportion of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.

mistakes.w: Lubrication increases efficiency because it gives the machine more energy.
mistakes.r: Lubrication reduces friction, so less energy is dissipated by heating.

mistakes.w: A device is 100% efficient if it is new.
mistakes.r: No real device is 100% efficient because some energy is always dissipated to the surroundings.

exam.q: State the equation linking efficiency, useful energy transferred and total energy supplied.
model: efficiency = useful energy transferred by the device / total energy supplied to the device
exam.tip: This equation must be recalled.

exam.q: Explain why efficiency has no units.
model: It is energy divided by energy, so the units (J / J) cancel.
exam.tip: Mention both quantities have the same unit.

exam.q: A motor is supplied with 800 J and transfers 600 J usefully. Calculate its efficiency.
model: efficiency = 600 / 800
exam.tip: Show the substitution for the first mark.

exam.q: A lamp is supplied with 1200 J. It wastes 960 J by heating. Calculate its percentage efficiency.
model: useful energy = 1200 - 960 = 240 J
efficiency = 240 / 1200 = 0.2
exam.tip: Find the useful energy first.

exam.q: An electric heater has an efficiency of 0.95. It is supplied with 5000 J. Calculate the useful energy transferred.
model: useful energy = 0.95 x 5000
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: A crane motor has an efficiency of 40%. It transfers 12 000 J to the gravitational potential store of a load. Calculate the total energy supplied.
model: Convert: 40% = 0.40
total = useful / efficiency = 12 000 / 0.40
exam.tip: Answer must be bigger than the useful energy.

exam.q: A student calculates the efficiency of a motor as 1.3. Explain why this must be wrong.
model: Efficiency cannot be greater than 1 (100%).
That would mean more useful energy out than was supplied, which breaks conservation of energy.
exam.tip: Refer to conservation of energy.

exam.q: Explain how lubricating the axle of a motor increases its efficiency.
model: Lubrication reduces friction at the axle.
So less energy is dissipated by heating the surroundings.
So a greater proportion of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.
exam.tip: End with 'greater proportion of input transferred usefully'.

exam.q: Suggest two ways of increasing the efficiency of an electric kettle and explain each.
model: Insulate the kettle body / use a material with low thermal conductivity.
This reduces energy transferred by heating from the kettle to the surroundings.
Fit a lid / keep the lid closed (or use a concealed element).
This reduces energy transferred to the air by convection/evaporation, so more heats the water.
exam.tip: Method plus reason for each pair of marks.

exam.q: A manufacturer wants to make a new car more efficient. Explain how efficiency is calculated and describe how the design of the car could be changed to increase its efficiency.
model: Efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy supplied (from the fuel).
Energy is wasted by friction between moving parts, air resistance, heating and sound.
Lubricating moving parts reduces friction so less energy is dissipated by heating.
Streamlining the body reduces air resistance so less work is done against it.
Insulating / reducing sound and vibration, or using a lighter body, reduces energy wasted.
So a greater proportion of the energy from the fuel is transferred to the kinetic store, increasing efficiency.
exam.tip: Start with the equation, then link each change to the pathway it reduces.

worked.q: An electric motor is supplied with 2.5 kJ of energy. It lifts a load, transferring 1800 J to the load's gravitational potential store. Calculate the efficiency as a decimal and a percentage.
steps: Convert to the same unit: 2.5 kJ = 2500 J.
efficiency = useful energy transferred / total energy supplied
efficiency = 1800 / 2500
efficiency = 0.72
Percentage: 0.72 x 100 = 72%

worked.q: A power station has an efficiency of 35%. It must supply 7000 MJ of useful electrical energy. How much energy must be supplied from the fuel, and how much is wasted?
steps: Convert: 35% = 0.35.
total energy supplied = useful energy / efficiency
wasted = total - useful = 20 000 - 7000 = 13 000 MJ
worked.ans: 20 000 MJ supplied from the fuel; 13 000 MJ is wasted.

worked.q: Motor A: input 500 J, useful output 350 J. Motor B: input power 200 W, useful output power 150 W. Which motor is more efficient?
steps: Motor A: efficiency = 350 / 500 = 0.70 (70%).
Motor B: efficiency = useful power / total power = 150 / 200 = 0.75 (75%).
0.75 is greater than 0.70.
worked.ans: Motor B is more efficient (75% compared with 70%).
